newsitem.title: UK: Dresdner move shows London's pulling power.
newsitem.headline: Dresdner move shows London's pulling power.

text.p: Dresdner Bank 's decision on Tuesday to run all of its Eurobond business from London is yet another sign of the strong gravitational pull the City of London exerts on the world's financial markets.

"I don't think the trend is going to move away from operations being centred on London. There are firm indications banks will keep on coming. The culture, legal framework and tradition of innovation are all important," one analyst said.

Dresdner, Germany's second largest commercial bank, also announced its investment banking arm Dresdner Kleinwort Benson was taking over London-based specialist bond boutique Luthy Baillie Dowsett Pethick & Co to cement the move.

"This is in line with the trend, not just from German banks but also from the Swiss, to build up business in London," John Leonard, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers in London said, adding that the Eurobond market had always been London-centred.

Eurobonds have proved an easy and popular way for companies, countries and supranationals to raise money as they are sold and traded internationally. The market grew up in London and has mushroomed into a multi-billion dollar business.
Dresdner's takeover of British merchant bank Kleinwort Benson was seen by many as an attempt to mimic the path taken by its great rival Deutsche Bank.

But some commentators said the latest purchase suggested it had not bought as big a Eurobond operation as it had wanted and therefore needed to supplement the Kleinwort team with an additional 15 staff and a new head in Peter Luthy.

Dresdner has not said it will move its combined investment banking operations lock-stock-and-barrel to London. This contrasts with Deutsche which took over Morgan Grenfell and some years later said it would base all its investment banking operations in London's traditional financial heartland.

It is currently building a large new headquarters for the Deutsche Morgan Grenfell operations and despite current problems in its asset management division, analysts pointed out it has restated its long-term commitment to the capital.
In July, Swiss financial group CS Holding said it would concentrate all investment and corporate banking in London.

Earlier this year Commerzbank said it would not shift its overall investment banking operations to London, preferring instead to step up its presence in both London and New York but keeping Frankfurt as the main headquarters.

Deregulation opened the London market up to large integrated investment banks in the 1980s and helped it steal a march on other financial centres such as Paris and Frankfurt and this momentum is continuing.
"The momentum has built up. The major operators have increased substantially since the 1980s," said the analyst who declined to be named.
He added that concerns that more sophisticated markets would dent London's pre-eminence were overblown. "There may be a dispersal, but there won't be a shift," he said.

Recent suggestions that London could be damaged if Britain does not join France and Germany in the first wave of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) have also been overdone and a delay could actually be in its favour, analysts said.
With Britain lagging its European neighbours in adopting the Euro, London would dominate even further foreign currency flows.
"The legal background is right and that's not going to change," the first analyst said.
